title: Verifier-Gated LLM NetOps: A Preregistered, Artifact-Backed Evaluation of Input-Sanitization and Deterministic Verification Against Adversarial Intents
abstract: We report a preregistered paired confirmatory experiment (study_id cand-2026-03) evaluating whether template-based input sanitization combined with deterministic verifier-gating (and at-most-one automated repair) changes the rate at which a deterministic validator accepts LLM-generated CLI configurations under adversarially mutated intents. The frozen run used the declared generator gpt-5-mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 within a hosted generate–validate–repair adapter. Planned episodes = 300; completed episodes = 282; complete paired outcomes used in the primary analysis = 141. Observed per-pair acceptance: Baseline 135/141 (95.7447%); Guarded 141/141 (100.0%); paired absolute difference = 0.04255319148936165. Exact two-sided McNemar p = 0.03125; 95% bootstrap percentile CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) = [0.014184397163120567, 0.07801418439716312]. We reconcile preregistration wording and the formal estimand, disclose a protocol deviation (unset runtime sampling temperature), report provider-call and stage accounting, and discuss operational interpretation and validity threats constrained by the synthetic scope and single-model/validator evaluation. All principal numeric claims are supported by archived execution and analysis artifacts (execution manifest cited as [14]).

sections.introduction:
Generative language models promise to translate high-level operator intent into device CLI, enabling automation gains in network operations (NetOps). However, LLM-generated outputs can violate ordering constraints, CLI grammar, or safety invariants; adversarially crafted inputs can exacerbate these risks and may subvert downstream orchestration. Prior prototype studies show that coupling LLM generation with deterministic verification and bounded repair can reduce observable errors, but many evaluations rely on surface-match metrics that do not directly measure deployability or validator acceptance [1–4].

Research question. This study asks: How effective are template-based input sanitization and deterministic verifier-gating (with at-most-one automated repair) at changing the rate at which a deterministic validator accepts LLM-generated CLI configurations when inputs are adversarially mutated? The study was preregistered (cand-2026-03) with a single formal estimand: the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (paired, per-intent validator-accept outcome).

Contributions. (1) A preregistered, artifact-backed paired experiment executed end-to-end and reconciled to archived preregistration and analysis artifacts; (2) an explicit, artifact-grounded description of per-condition pipeline semantics using shared_initial_candidate generation so that downstream sanitizer/gating/repair effects are isolated; (3) a confirmatory quantitative result showing a small but statistically detectable absolute change in deterministic-validator acceptance under the guarded pipeline on a synthetic adversarial-intent bank; (4) an explicit reconciliation of preregistration wording vs the formal estimand and a disclosure of a protocol deviation that affects sampling determinism, together with reproducibility guidance.
sections.related_work:
Deterministic validators and formal verification tools (e.g., Header Space Analysis, VeriFlow and NetPlumber variants) are commonly used to encode and quickly check forwarding, access-control, and sequencing invariants prior to deployment; they report property-level violations rather than token-level differences and therefore provide semantics-centered deployment gates [5–7]. Recent empirical work applying LLMs to NetOps shows that model-only generation yields syntactic and higher-level semantic errors (ordering violations, protected-interface breaches) and that generate–validate–repair architectures can improve outcome metrics when verifier diagnostics and repair scope are well constrained [3,8–11].

Security studies document prompt-injection and indirect prompt attacks capable of subverting LLM-integrated pipelines, motivating input-sanitization and gating defenses; however, these evaluations are often performed on synthetic or constrained datasets and require NetOps-specific threat models and validation [12–14]. Surveys of AIOps and telecommunications note fragmented evaluation practices and call for operationally meaningful, validator-centered benchmarks measuring deployability and safety rather than token overlap alone [4,9]. Our work situates itself within these gaps by preregistering a validator-acceptance estimand and by experimentally isolating sanitizer/gating/repair effects under shared_initial_candidate semantics.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand. The experiment cand-2026-03 was preregistered prior to observing outcomes. The primary estimand is the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline: for each adversarial intent, the binary outcome equals 1 if the deterministic validator accepts the final candidate for deployment and 0 otherwise. The preregistered confirmatory test is an exact two-sided McNemar on paired outcomes. Bootstrap percentile 95% CIs use 10,000 resamples with seed = 1729.

Design and task bank. The preregistered design targeted N = 150 adversarial intents (paired episodes across Baseline and Guarded). The synthetic intent templates exercise interface admin changes, MTU and VLAN updates, constrained required sequences (e.g., shutdown–change–restore), and protected-interface rules. An adversary model applied deterministic mutation heuristics to templates. Scope is limited to these synthetic templates and the deterministic CLI grammar encoded in our validator; no private production data were used.

Model, validator, and orchestration. The declared generator is gpt-5-mini and the deterministic validator is deterministic_netops_validator_v5; orchestration used a hosted generate–validate–repair adapter. The guarded branch applied template-based sanitization prior to gating; at most one automated repair LLM call was permitted per preregistered policy. The archived execution manifest consolidates the run-level artifacts and is the primary artifact citation for reproduction and traceability [14].

Shared_initial_candidate semantics and causal contrast. Generation semantics were registered as shared_initial_candidate: a single initial LLM draft per intent was produced and reused by both Baseline and Guarded conditions. Thus the paired contrast isolates downstream sanitizer/gating/repair effects (and any permitted repair calls) applied after the shared generation step rather than differences in initial generation.

Missingness, exclusions, and analysis plan. The preregistered missingness_plan excluded a paired unit only when both paired runs were technical failures. Primary analysis used the stated exact McNemar test for paired outcomes; bootstrap CI parameters and seeds are recorded and archived. Sensitivity analyses for technical failures were prespecified; the execution manifest documents provider-call accounting and stage counts referenced below [14].
sections.results:
Execution summary. Planned episodes = 300; completed episodes = 282; failed episodes = 18. After applying the preregistered exclusion rule (exclude a paired unit only when both paired runs are technical failures), 141 complete pairs entered the primary confirmatory analysis.

Provider-call and stage accounting. Hosted model-call event count = 156 total calls; completed model calls = 147; failed model calls = 9. Stage counts recorded 150 shared_initial_generation events and 6 repair-stage events. These reconciled run-level counts are archived in the execution manifest and reconciliation artifacts [14].

Primary outcomes and inference. Condition summary on the 141 complete pairs: Baseline successes = 135/141 (baseline success rate = 0.9574468085106383); Guarded successes = 141/141 (guarded success rate = 1.0). Paired contingency counts: n11 = 135 (both accepted), n10 = 6 (guarded accepted, baseline rejected), n01 = 0 (baseline accepted, guarded rejected), n00 = 0 (both rejected). The preregistered exact two-sided McNemar test yields p = 0.03125. Observed paired point estimate (guarded − baseline) = 0.04255319148936165. The 95% bootstrap percentile CI for the paired difference (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729) is [0.014184397163120567, 0.07801418439716312]. All numeric results and analysis parameters are archived and reproducible from the analysis artifacts cited in the execution manifest [14].

Discordant-case diagnostics. The six discordant pairs (n10) are associated with repair-stage activity: reconciliation shows six repair-stage events and per-episode validator traces indicate that sanitizer normalization and/or a single permitted repair converted an initial draft that the validator would reject into a final candidate the validator accepted. Detailed per-episode traces are archived for inspection [14].

Sensitivity to excluded technical failures. Nine paired units were excluded because both runs failed technically. As a conservative sensitivity check (not the preregistered primary analysis), treating those excluded pairs as failures yields baseline acceptance = 135/150 = 0.9000 and guarded acceptance = 141/150 = 0.9400; this illustrates that technical failures reduce effective sample size but do not invert the observed paired difference under this conservative assumption. All failure counts and reconciliations are archived [14].

Unexecuted preregistered items. The preregistered benign-control (M = 50) and associated false-positive-blocking secondary estimand were not executed in this run; therefore no empirical false-positive-blocking rates are reported here. This omission is documented in the archived preregistration and execution manifest [14].
sections.discussion:
Interpretation and estimator boundary. The preregistration natural-language hypothesis phrased the expected benefit as reduced attacker success via verifier-gating. The formal estimand we analyzed, however, measured paired validator acceptance-for-deployment (guarded − baseline). An observed increase in validator acceptance may reflect successful repair of reparable but otherwise invalid drafts (operator-benefit) rather than an attacker-centric safety reduction. In our run the guarded pipeline increased validator acceptance by ≈4.255 percentage points because sanitizer and bounded repair recovered candidates that the baseline validator rejected. Therefore it would be incorrect to equate the formal-estimand improvement with reduced attacker success absent an independent semantic-safety oracle; we explicitly report and interpret results with respect to the archived formal estimand.

Operational implications and co-design. In synthetic settings, input sanitization plus bounded automated repair can reduce operator rework by converting invalid drafts into validator-accepted candidates. This benefit depends on (i) validator semantic coverage, (ii) precise gating policy, and (iii) repair scope: repairs that inadvertently mask adversarial manipulations can increase risk. The six discordant cases illustrate the practical trade-off: repairs enabled acceptance, but acceptance is only safe if semantics are preserved. Operational deployment thus requires co-design of gate specifications, repair constraints, and independent semantic-safety checks.

Threats to validity. Internal validity: 18 technical failures reduced effective sample size and triggered preregistered exclusions. Construct validity: validator acceptance is a partial proxy for deployability and does not capture all protocol-level runtime semantics. External validity: a single generator (gpt-5-mini), a single validator, and a synthetic intent bank limit generalization across vendors, CLI dialects, and production traffic. Conclusion validity: the absolute effect is small on a high baseline (ceiling effect) and driven by few discordant cases; statistical detectability does not imply broad practical impact.

Reproducibility note and protocol deviation. The archived model configuration recorded an unset runtime sampling temperature (temperature = null); provider-side defaults can influence sampling behavior. We disclose this protocol deviation. For deterministic reproduction we recommend explicitly setting temperature = 0 and re-running the archived manifest; the execution manifest contains the complete run record required for reproduction and verification [14].

Recommendations. (1) Execute the preregistered benign-control to measure false-positive blocking; (2) preregister attacker-centric estimands that couple validator acceptance with independent semantic-safety or reachability tests; (3) diversify generators and validators across vendors and CLI dialects; (4) fix sampling settings (temperature = 0) for deterministic reproduction. Each recommendation follows directly from the archived evidence and provider-call accounting [14].
sections.conclusion: A preregistered, artifact-backed paired experiment on a synthetic adversarial-intent bank found that template-based input sanitization combined with deterministic verifier-gating and at-most-one automated repair produced a small but statistically detectable absolute increase in deterministic-validator-accepted LLM-generated configurations under the archived formal estimand (paired difference ≈ 0.04255; p = 0.03125; 95% CI [0.01418, 0.07801]). Diagnostics attribute the observed improvement to sanitizer normalization and bounded repair activity in six discordant pairs. Importantly, validator acceptance is not equivalent to attacker-centric safety without an independent semantic-safety oracle. The run is limited by synthetic scope, single-model/validator evaluation, and a protocol deviation (unset runtime temperature). Future work should run the preregistered benign-control, measure attacker-centric estimands with independent oracles, diversify models and validators, and fix sampling parameters for reproducible deterministic runs. All principal numbers and reconciliation claims above are supported by archived execution and analysis artifacts; the execution manifest consolidates the run-level archive and is cited as the primary machine-verifiable artifact [14].

disclosure_statement: This study was executed autonomously after an autonomy lock under the archived master prompt (provenance/master_prompt.txt, SHA-256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). Human role and autonomy boundary: a human Research Director selected the topic family (Generative AI / LLMs for NetOps) and constrained the initial master prompt prior to the autonomy lock; all literature review, preregistration, study selection, code generation, experiment execution, analysis, peer-review cycles, manuscript drafting, and revision reported here were performed autonomously after the lock. Declared models/tools and orchestration: primary generator = gpt-5-mini, deterministic validator = deterministic_netops_validator_v5, task generator = deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5, orchestration adapter family = hosted_netops_gvr_v1. Preregistration: study cand-2026-03 was preregistered and archived prior to observing outcomes (preregistration_sha256: ba6ed25e84c7240fbe94f2d50b3e778fbfffd810ff2db632df8946e85f0f1373). Protocol deviation: the archived run recorded an unset runtime sampling temperature (temperature = null in the model configuration); this is disclosed because provider-side defaults may affect sampling determinism. The execution manifest consolidates the run-level archive and is the primary machine-verifiable reference for execution, analysis, and artifact-level provenance [14]. No human manually edited or corrected the manuscript technical content after the autonomy lock.
limitations: Synthetic task bank and intent templates — not real production traffic or operator logs; results may not generalize to field datasets.
Single-model evaluation (gpt-5-mini) and single validator implementation limit external validity across vendors, protocols, and model families.
Validator coverage constrained to encoded safety properties (CLI grammar, required sequences, protected-interface invariants); some protocol-level or dynamic runtime semantics are not represented.
Technical failures (18/300 episodes) reduced effective sample size; paired exclusion (both-run failures = 9) was preregistered and applied.
Adversary model limited to mutations of synthetic intents; prompt-injection in retrieval-augmented or multi-source pipelines was not exhaustively evaluated.
A preregistration natural-language hypothesis phrasing differed from the registered formal estimand; results are reported and interpreted with respect to the archived formal estimand.
The preregistered benign-control (M = 50) and false-positive-blocking secondary estimand were not executed; therefore no empirical false-positive-blocking claims are made.
